text: Azure and AWS both run production workloads for most of the world's largest companies, and neither is simply better in the abstract. The question that actually matters, every time, is which provider fits this specific workload, for this specific team, right now. That has a real, defensible answer built from five factors — not a coin flip and not brand loyalty.

Five factors decide it. Existing team expertise, because ramp-up time and mistakes made while learning a new platform have a real dollar cost. Specific service capabilities, when one provider matches the workload better. Compliance and data residency, when data has to stay in a region or needs a certification one provider has and the other doesn't. Cost, measured for this workload's actual shape, not a general claim. And vendor lock-in — how hard it would be to leave this provider in three years.

Take an internal reporting tool built by a team that's run every other workload on Azure for five years, touching no regulated data, with modest and predictable load. Team expertise alone makes Azure the pragmatic choice here — there's no compliance or capability reason to introduce a second platform and a second set of operational skills for a workload this straightforward.

Now change one detail: the company acquires a startup whose analytics pipeline already runs on AWS-specific services nobody wants to rebuild. That's a genuine multi-cloud reason, and it's one of a small honest set: redundancy across providers when an outage is unacceptable, best-of-breed, picking the strongest service for a job even across providers, and inherited infrastructure from a merger nobody has consolidated yet.

What doesn't belong on that list is running two providers just because it's technically possible. Multi-cloud adds real operational complexity — a second console, a second set of skills, a second place things can go wrong — so it has to earn its place with one of those real reasons, not novelty.

You now have five honest factors for choosing a provider, and the real reasons some organizations genuinely run more than one. Next: taking whichever provider you land on and sizing its compute and storage from real expected load, instead of guessing at a number that sounds safe.
